subject: anatomy
title: Anterior abdominal wall and inguinal canal

steps.tx: The **rectus sheath** wraps the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles. It is made from the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Above the arcuate line, the sheath has an anterior and a posterior layer. Below the arcuate line, all aponeuroses pass in front of the muscle, so the posterior layer is absent. Only the transversalis fascia separates the muscle from the peritoneum there, which makes this region weaker.
steps.say: The rectus sheath wraps the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles. It is made from the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Above the arcuate line there is an anterior and a posterior layer. Below the arcuate line all the aponeuroses pass in front of the muscle, so there is no posterior layer. Only the transversalis fascia separates the muscle from the peritoneum there, which makes this area more prone to herniation.

steps.tx: The canal walls matter for exams. The **anterior wall** is mainly the external oblique aponeurosis, with fleshy internal oblique fibres in the lateral third. The **posterior wall** is the transversalis fascia, with the **conjoint tendon** in its medial third. The roof is the arching lower fibres of internal oblique and transversus. The floor is the inguinal ligament, with the lacunar ligament medially.
steps.say: The canal walls matter for exams. The anterior wall is mainly the external oblique aponeurosis, with fleshy internal oblique fibres in the lateral third. The posterior wall is the transversalis fascia, with the conjoint tendon in its medial third. The roof is formed by the arching lower fibres of internal oblique and transversus. The floor is the inguinal ligament, with the lacunar ligament medially.

rows: Lowest fibres join as conjoint tendon

steps.tx: The **conjoint tendon** forms by fusion of the lowest aponeurotic fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis. It lies in the posterior wall of the canal and joins the anterior rectus sheath medially. It strengthens the abdominal wall where the superficial ring weakens it. The conjoint tendon is not part of the floor and is not continuous with the inguinal ligament.
steps.say: The conjoint tendon forms by fusion of the lowest aponeurotic fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis. It lies in the posterior wall of the canal and joins the anterior rectus sheath medially. It strengthens the abdominal wall where the superficial ring weakens it. It is not part of the floor and is not continuous with the inguinal ligament.

vis.alt: Diagram of the four walls of the inguinal canal: anterior wall external oblique aponeurosis, posterior wall transversalis fascia with the conjoint tendon medially, roof arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis, floor inguinal ligament.
vis.caption: Walls of the canal: front external oblique, back transversalis fascia plus conjoint tendon, roof internal oblique and transversus, floor inguinal ligament.

steps.tx: Learn the **hernia** distinctions. An **indirect hernia** passes through the deep ring, lying lateral and anterior to the spermatic cord. A **direct hernia** bulges through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. **Hesselbach triangle** is bounded by the rectus abdominis medially, inferior epigastric artery laterally and the inguinal ligament below. A femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
steps.say: Learn the hernia distinctions. An indirect hernia passes through the deep ring and lies lateral and anterior to the spermatic cord. A direct hernia bulges through the posterior wall, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Hesselbach triangle is bounded by the rectus abdominis medially, the inferior epigastric artery laterally and the inguinal ligament below. A femoral hernia sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

steps.tx: Know the **spermatic cord** contents and nerves. The cord carries the ductus deferens, testicular and cremasteric arteries, pampiniform plexus and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve. The **cremaster muscle** comes from internal oblique. Cremasteric reflex is afferent through the femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve and efferent through the genital branch. Ilioinguinal nerve passes through the canal but is not part of the cord.
steps.say: Know the spermatic cord contents and nerves. The cord carries the ductus deferens, testicular and cremasteric arteries, pampiniform plexus and the genital branch of genitofemoral nerve. The cremaster muscle comes from internal oblique. The cremasteric reflex has an afferent limb through the femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve and an efferent limb through the genital branch. The ilioinguinal nerve passes through the canal but is not part of the cord.

vis.alt: Cross-section of the spermatic cord with three coverings from outside in: external spermatic fascia from external oblique, cremasteric fascia from internal oblique, internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia, enclosing the ductus deferens, arteries, pampiniform plexus and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve.
vis.caption: Three coverings, each borrowed from an abdominal wall layer; the ilioinguinal nerve lies on the cord, not inside it.
